Clonfert
klon-FURT
n. (the Galway see founded about 557 by Brendan the Navigator, with a famous Romanesque west doorway)
Irish Cluain Fearta, the meadow of the grave or of the miracle, from cluain, a meadow, and feart, a grave.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Clonfert in east Galway was founded about 557 by Brendan, who is buried there, and was a monastery, a school and then a diocese confirmed at Rathbreasail. Its cathedral keeps the most elaborate Romanesque doorway in Ireland, a gable of carved heads and chevrons from about 1180. Brendan himself is known chiefly from the Navigatio Sancti Brendani, a Latin voyage tale written three or four centuries after his death, in which he and his monks sail west for seven years, keep Easter on the back of a whale, and find the Land of Promise of the Saints; the book was one of the most widely copied works of the Middle Ages. Behind the legend there is a real and verifiable practice, the peregrinatio, by which Irish monks put to sea with no destination for the love of God, and reached the Hebrides, Orkney, the Faroes and Iceland. The dictionary records Clonfert for the sober fact inside the tale. The Psalter had already described these men before they sailed: those who go down to the sea in ships see the works of the LORD and his wonders in the deep.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a ship as a vessel of large size for navigation; the deep as the sea; an island as land surrounded by water; to escape as to flee from danger; and to renew as to make new again.

expand to see more

SHIP, n. In a general sense, a vessel or building of a peculiar structure, adapted to navigation; in strictness, a vessel with three masts.

DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean; any abyss or unfathomable gulf.

ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded by water; a body of land encompassed by the sea, a lake or a river.

ESCAPE, v.i. To flee from and avoid; to get out of the way; to be free or safe from danger.

RENEW, v.t. To renovate; to restore to a former state, or to a good state, after decay or depravation; to make new again.

Key Scripture

Psa 107:23 — "They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;"

Psa 107:24 — "These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep."

Isa 41:1 — "Keep silence before me, O islands; and let the people renew their strength: let them come near; then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment."

Act 28:1 — "And when they were escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita."

Modern Corruption

East Galway see founded about 557 by Brendan the Navigator, with Ireland's finest Romanesque doorway and the voyage legend that made it famous.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the voyage legend decorates and the Psalter states soberly, that the sea is a school for men who have to trust God in it. Of such men it is written, “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23), and the consequence is not adventure but sight: “These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:24).

The live temptation is to let a tall tale stand in for the real obedience underneath it. Irish monks did put to sea without a destination, and the islands they reached were real; the whale and the Land of Promise were not. Isaiah summons the islands to a hearing rather than to a legend: “Keep silence before me, O islands; and let the people renew their strength” (Isa 41:1). Luke's way of reporting a shipwreck is the right model for a voyage narrative, which is to name the place and move on: “then they knew that the island was called Melita” (Act 28:1).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew oniyah (H0591), a ship; Hebrew metsulah (H4688), the deep; Hebrew iy (H0339), an island; Greek nesos (G3520), an island.

expand to see more

Hebrew oniyah (H0591) — a ship; “They that go down to the sea in ships”, Psalm 107:23.

Hebrew maaseh (H4639) — a work, a deed; “These see the works of the LORD”, Psalm 107:24.

Hebrew metsulah (H4688) — a deep place, the depths; “and his wonders in the deep”, Psalm 107:24.

Hebrew chalaph (H2498) — to change, to renew; “let the people renew their strength”, Isaiah 41:1.

Greek nesos (G3520) — an island; “the island was called Melita”, Acts 28:1.

Usage

"“They that go down to the sea in ships” (Psa 107:23) — the real peregrini."

"“and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:24) — sight, not adventure."

"“Keep silence before me, O islands” (Isa 41:1) — a hearing, not a legend."
